title: Newton's Laws of Motion: A Return to Physics
summary: A short, practical reintroduction to Newton's three laws of motion for an adult coming back to physics. You will rebuild the ideas of force, inertia and acceleration from everyday examples and use them on simple problems.

audience.notes: Adults returning to physics after time away; comfortable with school algebra, no calculus assumed.

steer.focus: Build a working conceptual and quantitative grasp of Newton's three laws for an adult returning to physics, connecting everyday experience to the formal statements.
include: everyday worked examples such as cars, sport and walking
a clear distinction between mass and weight
simple vector reasoning about net force
exclude: rote mnemonics used in place of understanding

concepts.name: Net force
concepts.description: The net force on a body is the vector sum of all forces acting on it.
misconceptions: A force is needed to keep an object moving at constant velocity.
The largest single force, rather than the vector sum, decides how motion changes.

concepts.name: Inertia
concepts.description: Inertia is a body's resistance to any change in its state of motion.
misconceptions: Heavier objects fall faster in the absence of air resistance.
Inertia is itself a force that pushes objects.

concepts.name: Speed, velocity and acceleration
concepts.description: Speed, velocity and acceleration describe how a body's position and motion change over time.
misconceptions: Velocity and acceleration always point in the same direction.
An object with zero velocity must have zero acceleration.

concepts.name: Newton's first law
concepts.description: A body remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted on by a net force.
misconceptions: A moving object needs a continuous forward force to keep moving.
The first law only matters for objects that are standing still.

concepts.name: Inertial reference frame
concepts.description: An inertial frame is a reference frame in which Newton's first law holds.
misconceptions: Every reference frame is equally valid for applying Newton's laws.
The surface of the Earth is a perfectly inertial frame.

concepts.name: Newton's second law
concepts.description: The net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration (F = ma).
misconceptions: F = ma means a force sets an object's velocity rather than its acceleration.
Mass and weight are the same quantity.

concepts.name: Mass
concepts.description: Mass is the quantitative measure of a body's inertia and the m in F = ma.
misconceptions: An object's mass changes when it is moved to the Moon.
Mass is just another word for weight.

concepts.name: Newton's third law
concepts.description: When one body exerts a force on a second, the second exerts an equal and opposite force on the first.
misconceptions: Action and reaction act on the same object and therefore cancel out.
The larger or heavier object exerts the larger force.

lessons.title: The language of motion and the first law
lessons.summary: What force and inertia really mean, and why a moving object does not need a push to keep going.

steer.focus: Establish the vocabulary of motion and force and show why the first law reframes the everyday intuition that motion needs a cause.
include: the difference between velocity and acceleration

modules.title: Force, inertia and the quantities of motion
modules.summary: Net force, inertia, and the difference between speed, velocity and acceleration.

steer.focus: Give precise meanings to net force, inertia and the kinematic quantities before any law is stated.
include: the vector nature of force and velocity

objectives.title: Explain net force and inertia
objectives.statement: The learner can explain net force and inertia and why together they govern how motion changes.

objectives.title: Distinguish speed, velocity and acceleration
objectives.statement: The learner can distinguish speed, velocity and acceleration and relate them to a body's changing motion.

modules.title: Newton's first law and inertial frames
modules.summary: Newton's first law and the reference frames in which it holds.

steer.focus: State Newton's first law and the idea of an inertial frame, correcting the intuition that a steady force is needed for steady motion.
include: why a passenger lurches when a bus brakes
exclude: quantitative force balance requiring F = ma

objectives.title: Apply Newton's first law to bodies in equilibrium
objectives.statement: The learner can apply Newton's first law to describe bodies at rest or in uniform straight-line motion.

objectives.title: Identify inertial reference frames
objectives.statement: The learner can identify reference frames in which Newton's first law holds and where it appears to fail.

lessons.title: The second and third laws in use
lessons.summary: How net force sets acceleration, and how every force comes in a pair.

steer.focus: Introduce the quantitative second law and the reciprocal third law, and use them together on simple systems.
include: F = ma applied to one-body problems
exclude: multi-body free-body diagrams with friction and tension networks

modules.title: Newton's second law: F = ma
modules.summary: Newton's second law, F = ma, and the role of mass.

steer.focus: Make F = ma concrete: net force sets acceleration, mass resists it, and the units tie together.
include: the SI units of force, mass and acceleration

objectives.title: Explain F = ma and the role of mass
objectives.statement: The learner can explain Newton's second law, F = ma, and the role of mass as a measure of inertia.

objectives.title: Calculate acceleration from net force
objectives.statement: The learner can calculate the acceleration of a simple one-body system from the net force and the mass.

modules.title: Newton's third law: action and reaction
modules.summary: Newton's third law and the action-reaction pairs it describes.

steer.focus: Explain the third law and the frequent error of thinking action-reaction pairs cancel.
exclude: momentum conservation as a formal topic

objectives.title: Apply Newton's third law to action-reaction pairs
objectives.statement: The learner can apply Newton's third law to identify the equal and opposite pairs in an interaction.
